note: The product's baseline: rules that make sense on every developer machine. Do not
edit it for one organisation or machine; put that into config/org.json or
config/local.<host>.json, which may add facts, tighten rules and, with a reason and
an expiry date, make exceptions (docs/design-notes.md, 8). build.py merges the three files
into policy.json, which hooks/guard.py reads, and managed-settings.json.
What does NOT belong here: what counts as a read-only command, which options of
find/sed/tar start a program, how a dependency is recognised in a manifest. That
knowledge is about how programs behave and lives in hooks/guard.py.
One entry per own domain (added by the organisation layer), with the purposes it
serves. build.py fans these out into sandbox.network.allowedDomains (purpose
'network'), the WebFetch list in the hook ('webfetch') and the auto-mode text
('trusted'), so the three lists cannot drift apart.
Design notes 3: reading on these hosts is free, every change asks. Design notes 2 adds
that reads which send data out, or read secrets or personal data, ask as well.
A new server goes in known_hosts AND here.
Become managed additionalDirectories (design notes, 9). guard.py uses the list
to decide where a git network command may run without a question (design notes, 4):
those commands run outside the sandbox, and Claude's temp folders are not on it.
roots: folders inside the home folder whose git checkouts the sandbox opens when a
session starts in one ("." in allowRead); elsewhere inside the read boundary the
hook denies shell commands (design notes, 12). Empty: only the paths above.
Projects scripts/patch-scan.sh checks (/patch-check), relative to root.
Read only by the script, not by the hook.
Decided 2026-11-20. Everything read on a server goes to the model provider, so
the read/write split alone was not enough: the auto-mode text said credentials
and personal data must not leave the servers, while the hook let them be read.
This is the rule both now follow. Only the lists are configurable; how a command
is recognised stays in guard.py.
secret_files: real key and credential files. A certificate is public, so
cert.pem and fullchain.pem stay free; a .pem counts only when its name or folder
says private. Other config files with passwords in them (Prosody, Jitsi,
wp-config.php) stay free on purpose: they are needed for troubleshooting.
personal_files: the logs with the most personal data. Error logs, journalctl,
syslog and Jitsi logs stay free, so troubleshooting works without questions.
Design notes 6. require_sfw: installs only run through Socket Firewall.
sfw_works_in_sandbox: sfw 1.16.0 ignores the sandbox proxy (tested 2026-11-15),
so while this is false an install in the sandbox is denied right away and handed
to the user's terminal. Set it to true once sfw works there.

credentials.note: Paths and variables the sandbox keeps away from every command.

note: Tools that always ask, whatever the hook says, and that run outside the sandbox
(they need the keychain or a local socket). Both lists are generated from this.
Paths inside the read boundary (read_boundary) that commands in the sandbox may
still read: tool caches, single configuration files, never whole folders that can
hold tokens (design notes, 12). ~/.npmrc and ~/.composer are not here on purpose:
the package protection comes through env, Composer runs outside the sandbox.
build.py expands a leading ~ to the home of the user who builds, a leading
@darwin_user_temp_dir to that folder. xcrun_db there is the tool cache of the Xcode
shims /usr/bin/python3 and /usr/bin/git (paths of developer tools, no data); without
it every call starts xcodebuild, takes 1.7 s and reports EPERM (v1.1.4).
Design notes 12. Where reading ends, for commands in the sandbox (denyRead) and for
Read, Grep and Glob (hooks/guard.py). Inside these roots only the working
directories, sandbox.allow_read and, for the file tools, file_tools_extra are
readable. Replaces blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories, whose static proof asked
for nearly every shell command. @darwin_user_dir, @darwin_user_temp_dir and
@darwin_user_cache_dir are the per-user data, temporary and cache folders of all
apps under /private/var/folders (getconf DARWIN_USER_DIR, _TEMP_DIR, _CACHE_DIR).
The Linux list is generated but not yet tested (bubblewrap behaves differently).
Design notes 12. MCP servers run outside the sandbox with the user's rights. With
restrict_servers, managed settings allow only the servers in allowed_servers
(allowedMcpServers, by server name); an empty list then allows none. List the
servers in use first with ./build.py --audit.
Decision log of the hook (design notes, 1). Logged are ask and deny, plus silent ssh
and git network calls, so the rules can be tuned from real sessions. The command
is cut to max_command_chars and obvious secrets are redacted.
Rule ids listed here only log 'would have asked' instead of asking. For trying
out a new rule before it goes live; the fixes of design notes 2 are live right away
(decided 2026-11-20). Ids are the ones in the decision log.

webfetch.note: Hosts the WebFetch tool may use without a question; own domains are added.

note: Design notes 9. lock_lower_scopes: managed settings are the only source of permission
rules and sandbox read paths (allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly,
allowManagedReadPathsOnly). Rules from ~/.claude/settings.json, project settings,
/permissions and 'Yes, and don't ask again' then no longer apply; deny and ask rules
a project brings along must be added here. Check first with ./build.py --audit.
working_directories become permissions.additionalDirectories in managed settings.
required_minimum_version: the oldest Claude Code that knows every key we set
(blockWritesOutsideWorkingDirectories needs 2.1.314; sandbox denyRead with allowRead
inside it, the read boundary of design notes 12, needs 2.1.329).
Names install.sh and uninstall.sh use on this machine. The label names the LaunchAgent
of the ssh-agent (design notes, 10); to change it, run uninstall.sh first.
